newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia eyes NATO in diplomatic offensive.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia eyes NATO in diplomatic offensive.

text.p: Slovenia, the former Yugoslav republic that broke away from Belgrade in a 10-day war in 1991, is pinning its hopes on being among the first ex-communist states to be invited to join NATO in July.

While the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary are tipped as frontrunners for the first wave of NATO's eastward expansion, some analysts believe Slovenia and Romania may also be chosen at a summit of the Western military alliance in Madrid in July.
Slovenia has launched a diplomatic offensive in the past few months to try to win a ticket into the 16-member alliance. Neighbouring Italy has become Ljubljana's firmest backer.
Opinion polls over the past 18 months have shown up to 71 percent of Slovenians supporting membership of NATO, with up to 28 percent against.
"The public is most opposed to a possibility of foreign armed forces being placed in Slovenia, but there is a very small chance that would happen," one defence analyst said.

Reasons for embracing Slovenia into NATO range from geographical -- it provides a land link from Italy to Hungary -- to strategic. Proponents says it would demonstrate to other ex-Yugoslav states, Croatia in particular, the advantages of a firm democracy, full human rights and a free-market economy.
Far from burdening the country's economy with extra costs, government officials and analysts believe membership, estimated at around $10 million, would work out cheaper in the long run.

"The cost of $10 million does not include the cost of modernising the army which will be necessary whether we join NATO or not and could be more expensive if we stay out," Gorazd Vidrih, an adviser at the Ministry of Defence, told Reuters.

In 1996, Slovenia's defence spending was 2.1 percent of GDP or about $310 million. The government has not yet set the budget for 1997 but some analysts expect a rise of five to 10 percent in defence spending.

"Although the exact cost cannot be calculated as yet, joining NATO would be good, because it would improve Slovenia's security, its international reputation and would therefore also enhance its economic credibility," said Vinko Vegic of Ljubljana University's Faculty of Social Sciences.
The Slovenian army has yet to be fully restructured from its role as a territorial defence backup to the Yugoslav army with only 10 percent of professional soldiers to a modern outfit.
Since a United Nations arms embargo on former Yugoslav republics was lifted in June last year, Slovenia has begun to upgrade its army and set up a proper air force and navy.
As Ljubljana moves to make its armed forces more professional, the defence ministry sees numbers falling from about 56,000 now to between 35,000 and 40,000 in the next five years.
The number of career soldiers is expected to rise to between 6,000 and 8,000 from 4,100 currently.
